title: When Too Many Cooks Spoil the Broth: Three Failure Modes of Multi-Agent LLM Reliability
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems are widely deployed under three implicit assumptions: that self-confidence calibration transfers to peer evaluation, that errors made by distinct instances are statistically independent, and that any sufficiently calibrated model is an equivalent verifier. We test all three across GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Llama-3.3-70B. Self-confidence and peer-resistance dissociate: Claude shows the strongest self-confidence signal yet accepts every deliberately-wrong peer output, the opposite of what unidimensional calibration predicts. Four independent GPT-4o instances agree on the same wrong answer \(56\%\) of the time on obscure factual queries versus \(0.4\%\) predicted under independence—a \(140\times\) violation. A pre-registered cross-family replication ( \(N=200\) , three architecturally distinct families) yields \(55\%\) three-way agreement, statistically indistinguishable from the same-family baseline (one-sided binomial \(p=0.41\) ): family diversification does not reduce correlated hallucination. Verifier choice produces a 42-percentage-point spread in error propagation. We propose a three-phase framework treating self-confidence assessment, peer-resistance capability, and error correlation as orthogonal axes requiring distinct training signals, and identify query-inherent rarity, not shared training, as the dominant driver of correlated failure.

title: Tools and architectures for agentic systems in clinical AI and radiology
venue: European Journal of Radiology Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming medical imaging, particularly through the integration of large language models, especially large multimodal models that process both text and imaging data. A new paradigm known as agentic AI uses embedded LLMs within software systems to observe, reason, and act autonomously over time. These systems often operate within iterative control loops that enable decision-making, tool use, and interaction with external data sources. An extension of this concept is the multi-agent system (MAS), in which multiple specialized agents collaborate to solve complex tasks through communication and coordination. These architectures are particularly relevant to radiology, where workflows involve multiple stages, including imaging acquisition, report generation, clinical decision support, and quality assurance. However, despite growing interest and rapid technical progress, most agentic AI systems, including multi-agent architectures, in healthcare remain research-use-only technologies that have not yet undergone sufficient prospective validation or regulatory approval for widespread autonomous clinical deployment. This article reviews the current technological landscape of agentic and multi-agent architectures, describes the underlying system components and orchestration patterns, and evaluates the major frameworks for building such systems. We further discuss emerging interoperability standards and infrastructure for observability and reliability, and consider how these architectures may enable future clinical decision support systems and automated imaging workflows.

title: VISH-GUARD: a multi-agent and LLM-powered framework for multilingual voice phishing detection
abstract: Voice phishing (vishing) has emerged as a major cybersecurity threat, leveraging persuasive speech and psychological manipulation to deceive victims in real time. Existing detection approaches remain limited by monolingual assumptions, unimodal analysis, and poor interpretability, reducing their effectiveness against adaptive and multilingual attacks. This paper presents VISH-GUARD, a multi-agent vishing detection framework that combines multimodal analysis with large language model (LLM)-based reasoning to achieve robust, multilingual, and explainable threat detection. The system coordinates specialized agents responsible for acoustic feature analysis, semantic intent recognition, emotion detection, and behavioral profiling. Their outputs are integrated into a unified risk assessment, while an LLM-based reasoning layer generates structured explanations to support human analysts. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce a new annotated dataset of synthetic yet realistic vishing calls in English, French, and Arabic, incorporating background noise, emotional cues, and diverse persuasion strategies. Experimental results show that VISH-GUARD achieves an F1-score of 0.96, outperforming unimodal agents, multimodal deep learning baselines, and an end-to-end multimodal transformer baseline, while reducing false negatives in scenarios involving emotional manipulation and behavioral irregularities. Overall, VISH-GUARD demonstrates how multi-agent collaboration combined with LLM-driven reasoning can provide an effective and transparent defense against modern voice phishing attacks.

title: From detection to action: Using LLM agents for Fault-Tolerant Control
abstract: We propose an agentic Large Language Model (LLM) framework for active Fault-Tolerant Control (FTC) that transforms fault detection outputs into constraint-aware recovery actions grounded in plant-specific knowledge. The approach couples (i) a multi-agent workflow that decomposes operator duties into monitoring, planning, action synthesis, simulation, validation, and reprompting; (ii) a Digital Process Plant Twin (DPPT) that exposes plant data, models, and a simulation service for pre-execution testing; and (iii) a Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Graph RAG) layer built on the CPSMod ontology, which organizes plant knowledge (structure, function, hybrid dynamics, control context, and fault semantics) into a graph that supports relation-aware, multi-hop retrieval for the agents. Corrective actions are generated as minimal-risk state-machine recovery paths and corresponding discrete commands or continuous setpoint adaptations, then validated deterministically against interlocks, envelopes, and dynamic feasibility before any actuation. If no acceptable plan is found within a bounded time window, control is handed to a deterministic fallback policy. The framework is evaluated exclusively in simulation on two representative benchmarks: a discrete batch Mixing Module and a Continuous Stirred-Tank Reactor (CSTR) under closed-loop PID regulation. The evaluation isolates the detection-to-action step under a matched-model assumption: the DPPT used for pre-execution validation is identical to the model generating the simulated plant behavior and uses the same injected fault configuration. Robustness to plant-model mismatch and sensor-noise variation or misspecification is not evaluated in this study. Results with lightweight LLMs (GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4.1-mini) show that semantically grounded agents can derive recovery decisions that satisfy the configured validation criteria within latency budgets compatible with the respective process dynamics, demonstrating a pathway from detection to validated corrective action under this matched-model simulation setting.

title: ADVERSARIAL RESILIENCE OF AGENTIC INFRASTRUCTURE-AS-CODE SYSTEMS: THREAT MODEL, ATTACK TAXONOMY, AND MULTI-LAYERED DEFENSE ARCHITECTURE
abstract: The integration of large language models (LLMs) and agentic components into Infrastructure as Code (IaC) workflows significantly expands the attack surface of cloud automation environments. This paper proposes a threat model for agentic IaC systems in the form of the structure SIaC = (Agents, Environment, Configurations, Outcomes), which makes it possible to identify the critical points of influence: agent input data, configuration state, agent intents and goals, inter-agent communication channels, the execution process, authorization mechanisms, and system availability. Based on this model, a taxonomy of 40 attack vectors grouped into 7 categories is developed: prompt injection, configuration state poisoning, agent intent manipulation, attacks on inter-agent communication, exploitation of execution failures, attacks on authorization and access control, and attacks on integrity and availability. A multi-layered (compositional) defense architecture is proposed that combines input validation, agent intent verification, coordination and consensus mechanisms, and self-healing capabilities. The research methodology comprises three stages: threat modeling based on literature synthesis and a preliminary expert review (a formal Delphi study with an external panel is left to future work); design of the compositional defense architecture; and empirical validation in a reproducible software package on 2,157 scenarios — 1,441 synthetic domain-specific scenarios covering all 7 taxonomy categories (each represented by more than 100 scenarios) and 716 scenarios from public datasets (deepset/prompt-injections and labelled Terraform fixtures from the KICS project, both Apache-2.0) — under 1-, 3-, and 5-agent cluster configurations. The defense mechanisms are implemented as deterministic checks (rules, policies, cryptographic integrity), ensuring full reproducibility. The aggregate detection rate on the synthetic scenarios is 79.9% (95% CI 77.3–82.3%) with a false positive rate of 0.7%; effectiveness differs across categories, with the lowest results for agent intent manipulation (A3, 64.7%) and inter-agent communication (M4, 66.7%). On an independent real-world injection set (deepset) the domain-tuned rules detect only 14.4% of attacks, and non-English injections are not detected at all, which demonstrates the limited cross-domain transferability of static rules. Conversely, in a live LLM-agent loop (AgentDojo) on a domain-specific IaC benchmark the defense reduces the attack success rate from 50.0% to 16.7% and raises utility under attack from 66.7% to 91.7%, confirming its effectiveness within the target domain. All 40 attack vectors are additionally mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK, MITRE ATLAS, CWE, CVSS 4.0, NIST CSF 2.0, and OWASP frameworks; ATT&CK and ATLAS prove complementary (92.5% combined coverage), as the LLM-agent-specific vectors are covered by ATLAS. We formally prove composition properties (detection monotonicity, a union bound on false positives) and consensus correctness restoration under up to f < n/2 compromised agents. Future work includes a fully machine-checked verification of these properties and expansion of the attack scenario set.

title: Semantic Drift in Autonomous Agents: Detecting Runtime Goal Mutation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
abstract: Autonomous large language model (LLM) agents extend the attack surface beyond classical input-output filtering. Tool outputs, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) chunks, inter-agent messages, and persistent memory constitute internal trust boundaries that adversaries exploit through indirect prompt injection, RAG poisoning, semantic goal drift, and multi-turn crescendo jailbreaks. We present GuardAgent Runtime, a framework-agnostic middleware that interposes on agent execution, enforces zero-trust inspection of all untrusted data flows, and maintains runtime intent continuity relative to the user’s authorized objective. GuardAgent composes pattern-based injection detection, embedding-based semantic drift and intent verification (Shadow Critic), multi-layer RAG inspection, and a temporally decaying risk accumulation engine with crescendo trend detection. We formalize detection scores and policy mapping, describe an open-source implementation with LangGraph/CrewAI/AutoGen adapters, and evaluate on a 20-scenario adversarial benchmark plus a browser pre-submit extension. With isolated per-scenario evaluation, GuardAgent achieves 90.0% F1 (90.0% precision, 90.0% recall), 100% accuracy on RAG poisoning and benign corpora, and mean interception latency under 4 ms excluding cold-start embedding load.

title: Detecting Collusion in LLM-based Multi-agent Financial Decision Systems: A Conditional-mutual-information Detector and a Modular Oversight Architecture
venue: International journal of intelligent engineering and systems
abstract: Large language model agents increasingly review the same financial cases in parallel, and agreement between them may reflect shared evidence or covert coordination.We detect covert coordination from the agents' outputs alone, with no access to model internals or inter-agent messages.A conditional mutual information test checks whether two agents' scores remain dependent once the shared input is conditioned out; independent competent agents leave no residual dependence, coordinated agents do.The detector is the validated component of a proposed modular oversight architecture that specifies uncertainty decomposition, calibrated escalation, and incentive-compatible scoring.On synthetic regimes the false-positive rate is consistent with the 0.05 level and detection power reaches 0.980 at moderate coordination strength.On real credit data scored by Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-4o, the test flagged coordination in all 15 runs and raised none on honest competence, while correlation baselines flagged honest agreement and a language-model auditor caught 4 of 15.

title: EMPIRICAL COMPARISON OF AGENT COMMUNICATION PROTOCOLS FOR TASK ORCHESTRATION
abstract: Context. The problem of comparative evaluation of communication protocols for task orchestration by large language model (LLM) agents is considered. The object of study is the process of interaction between LLM agents and external tools, as well as between autonomous LLM agents, during task orchestration.Objective. The goal of this work is to develop a systematic pilot benchmark comparing tool integration, multi-agent delegation, and hybrid architectures for standardized queries at three levels of complexity, and to quantify the advantages and disadvantages in terms of response time, context window consumption, cost, error recovery, and implementation complexity.Method. An open-source health analyzer application was developed to query four public data sources for repository statistics, package downloads, vulnerability data, and community metrics. Thirty queries were run five times for each architecture at three levels of complexity, resulting in 450 fail-safe executions. The same large language model was used in all executions. The statistical analysis used bootstrap confidence intervals, the Mann-Whitney test with Bonferroni correction, and Cliff’s delta effect sizes.Results. A statistically significant crossover effect was found: the tool integration protocol is faster for simple queries, but the multi-agent protocol outperforms on complex multi-project comparisons, consuming fewer tokens through distributed context windows, resulting in lower cost. The hybrid architecture tracks the winner at each level of complexity with near-optimal performance.Conclusions. The scientific novelty is an empirical demonstration that the two protocols exhibit a complexity-dependent performance crossover, showing that they complement each other rather than compete. Context-window bloat in single-agent architectures is quantified for the first time in a pilot case study. The practical significance is a validated decision framework: using a tool integration protocol for single-source queries, a multi-agent protocol for complex orchestration, and a hybrid routing when complexity is unknown at runtime. Directions for further research include extending the benchmark to additional models, distributed deployments, and additional application domains

title: Trust-Weighted Adaptive Consensus: A Resilient Coordination Framework for Next-Generation Large Language Model Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have moved from singleturn assistants to persistent, tool-using systems that plan, delegate, and cooperate.This shift has produced an explosion of multi-agent system (MAS) frameworks, interoperability protocols, and orchestration patterns, yet production deployments continue to report failure rates far higher than single-agent baselines.This paper synthesizes the current state of AI agents and multi-agent systems as of mid-2026, organizes the coordination design space into a four-part topology taxonomy, and reviews the emerging empirical literature on why multi-agent systems fail.Building on documented gaps, particularly the absence of adaptive, trust-aware coordination in widely used frameworks.We propose Trust-Weighted Adaptive Consensus (TWAC), a coordination-layer mechanism that combines capability-aware sparse shortlisting, an exponentially-weighted per-agent trust ledger, and uncertainty-gated verification.We evaluate TWAC against round-robin and centralized-auction baselines in a controlled simulation across 500 tasks and 30 independent trials.TWAC improves task success rate while reducing communication overhead relative to full-broadcast coordination and lowering cascading-failure rates by more than an order of magnitude.We conclude with future research implications for trust-based coordination in agentic AI systems.

title: LLM-Driven Multi-Agent Control for Skill-Based Smart Manufacturing
venue: IEEE International Conference on Emerging Technologies and Factory Automation (ETFA)
abstract: Factories are shifting toward smaller lot sizes with high product customization, requiring frequent re-programming of flexible and reconfigurable automation systems. LLM-based agents can be deployed in two complementary roles: Offline, they generate deterministic production sequences, reducing programming effort; online, they operate live machines and handle unforeseen runtime faults that static programs cannot anticipate. We propose a solution in which each factory module is paired with a dedicated LLM-based agent and an MCP tool server that exposes the module's skills via OPC UA method calls, with agents coordinating over MQTT and grounded by real-time updates of the factory state. We compare three agent architectures (orchestrator, peer-to-peer, and monolithic) across nine production challenges of increasing complexity in a simulation of a physical six-module hexagonal factory, including silent hardware fault detection. The monolithic and peer-to-peer architectures both achieve the highest mean solve rate (93\%), while the orchestrator uniquely resolves a silent conveyor-belt fault in all ten runs by autonomously rerouting plates around the blocked segment. All architectures exhibit emergent fault-diagnosis behavior without any explicit failure-handling logic, establishing standardized MCP tooling, MQTT-based inter-agent communication, and real-time state injection as a viable and reproducible foundation for LLM-programmed smart manufacturing.

title: Preventing Error Propagation in Multi-Agent AI through Runtime Monitoring
venue: International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications
abstract: Multi-agent AI systems can improve answer selection by allowing different language models to exchange reasoning traces, revise initial predictions, and support a final decision. However, such communication may also introduce reliability risks: reasoning from one agent can correct another agent’s mistake, but it can also mislead an agent that was initially correct. This paper studies reliable multi-agent AI communication through reasoning exchange and runtime answer revision. We develop a framework in which agents first answer multiple-choice questions independently, then share reasoning traces and revise their decisions. We conduct numerical experiments where we evaluate whether this process improves accuracy, produces more positive than negative answer transitions, and remains effective across domains such as cybersecurity, networking, and general knowledge. The results help identify when multi-agent reasoning improves reliability and when it may propagate errors.

title: AgentFuzz: Trace-Level Fuzzing for Prompt Spillover in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
venue: International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications
abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed inside multi-agent systems (MAS), where specialized agents communicate through natural language to perform perception, memory retrieval, planning, verification, and execution. This collaboration improves capability but also creates a new attack surface: adversarial instructions injected into a low-trust upstream channel can silently propagate across agents and influence downstream high-privilege decisions. We call this phenomenon prompt spillover. Existing prompt fuzzers mainly target single-model jailbreaks and therefore fail to capture vulnerabilities that emerge from inter-agent communication. To address this gap, we present AgentFuzz, a framework for discovering prompt spillover attacks in LLM-based MAS. Given a target MAS, a low-trust injection channel, and a deterministic safety oracle, AgentFuzz searches for prompts that produce unsafe, executable, and verifier-approved action plans. The search uses MAS-native mutation operators selected online by a multi-armed bandit, while a trace-level composite reward, computed over the full inter-agent communication trace rather than only the final output, provides dense feedback on propagation, verifier bypass, and executable validity. We evaluate AgentFuzz across three LLM backbones, three MAS topologies, and five injection channels. On a five-agent linear MAS with no defense, AgentFuzz’s optimized attacks reach 35.2% ASR, outperforming PromptFuzz (26.8%) and LLM-Fuzzer (23.1%) on the same configuration. Similar improvements are observed in verifier bypass, executable validity, and spillover rate. Our results show that prompt spillover is a structural communication-layer vulnerability in MAS and motivate trace-aware defenses for secure MAS deployment.

title: A Survey on Agentic Security: Applications, Threats and Defenses
abstract: In this work we present the first holistic survey of the agentic security landscape, structuring the field around the fundamental pillars of Applications, Threats and Defenses. We provide a comprehensive taxonomy of 274 papers that covers red-teaming, blue-teaming and domain-specific applications, attack surfaces on agentic systems, defense techniques, and both offensive and defensive evaluation frameworks. For each pillar, we first discuss the literature around the taxonomy and then perform a quantitative analysis to understand the patterns across these works. For the applications, we show their security-lifecycle coverage map, compare between red-teaming and blue-teaming agents, and analyze the adversarial use of red-teaming applications. On the threat side, we analyze the entry points and agent-loop stages that attacks target, their specificity to the agentic setting, and the threat models they assume. On the defense side, we analyze the prevailing defense strategies, their cost and security trade-offs, and where in the agent lifecycle they are deployed. Finally, we provide a deatiled cross-cutting analysis, where we map which defenses cover which attack classes and chart trends in agent architecture, backbone model usage, and data modality coverage. Taken together, these findings give a researcher a structural understanding of how agentic capabilities, vulnerabilities, and countermeasures relate to one another, and to identify where the field is concentrated and where it is thin.

title: Adaptive Retrieval Augmented Generation with Graph Based Knowledge Structures and Multi Agent Orchestration: A Comprehensive Review and Proposed Framework
venue: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
abstract: Large Language Models have become integral to enterprise knowledge systems, yet their propensity to produce factually ungrounded outputs termed hallucinations remains a critical obstacle in regulated deployments. Retrieval Augmented Generation grounds model outputs in external knowledge, but conventional vector based pipelines exhibit severe limitations in multi hop reasoning and deterministic verification. While recent literature explores Graph based RAG and Agentic RAG as independent solutions, their isolated deployments fail to resolve the underlying tradeoffs between structural rigidity and non deterministic overhead. This paper presents a comprehensive literature review of the current RAG landscape, mapping the architectural evolution from static retrieval to dynamic multi agent orchestration. A rigorous comparative analysis evaluates these paradigms across retrieval adaptivity, multi hop capability, and hallucination mitigation. Through critical analysis, this work identifies persistent research gaps regarding graph construction noise, static retrieval policies, and the self correction paradox in LLMs. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a technically rigorous Proposed Framework: An Adaptive Agentic GraphRAG architecture. The proposed methodology leverages a LangGraph state machine to orchestrate planner and verifier agents across a hybrid vector graph backend, introducing extrinsic algorithmic verification to solve the self correction paradox. This paper serves as a theoretical foundation and architectural proposal intended for future experimental validation in enterprise environments.

title: Top-Down Multi-agent LLM System with Runtime Data for MISRA C Violation Detection
venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)
abstract: Ensuring MISRA C compliance is crucial for the safety and reliability of embedded software. For this purpose, industries utilize static rule checkers but suffer high ratios of both missed violations and false alarms. Although companies also try to utilize LLMs for this purpose, existing LLM-based approaches have suboptimal performance for large, complex programs. We introduce LASIK, the world-first top-down multi-agent LLM compliance-checking framework for MISRA C, which combines on-demand repository-level context provision with runtime execution evidence. This design enables LASIK to report more true violations than state-of-the-art static analyzers and a naive vanilla LLM approach, while maintaining a low false positive ratio. Our evaluation on 10 embedded projects shows that LASIK detects 1.3-2.7 times more true violations than the static analyzers and the vanilla LLM approach, while achieving the lowest false alarm ratio (26.7%). Furthermore, on an industrial software developed by VPlusLab Inc., LASIK detects up to 2.1 times more true violations with a low false alarm rate (i.e., 10.8%) than the baseline techniques.

title: A Deep Learning Framework for Evaluating and Mitigating Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
abstract: In the world of large language models (LLMs), prompt injection attacks are a severe security risk that can circumvent the instructions given to AI agents and potentially cause damage. In agentic architectures, the vulnerabilities are magnified because of the increased attack surfaces which are present in the use of tools, APIs and chains of reasoning. The vulnerabilities are compounded in agentic architectures as the tools used, APIs called, and chains of reasoning become a larger attack surface, resulting in an increased sense of unreliability. Paraphrased, adaptive, and context-aware attacks are not thwarted by rule-based and static prompt engineering defenses. This paper introduces a deep learning-based approach to detecting and thwarting prompt injection attacks in LLM agent systems. Uses a hybrid model of known and customer-generated adversarial prompts to combine transformer-based classification, semantic risk-scoring and adaptive mitigation procedures. Stratified data splits are used in the experiments, as are synthetic attack generation and rule-based, BERT and zero-shot LLM classifiers. In terms of precision, recall, F1 score and AUC, the proposed framework is found to be better than all the baselines. Attack of instruction override, data extraction and tool misuse are greatly enhanced and resistant to adversarial scenarios that are not seen and adaptable. The mitigation module achieves high task utility; low false positive rates and the high success rate of the attacks is significantly reduced. Overall, the framework demonstrates that it is possible to integrate detection, risk estimation, and mitigation in a single pipeline, resulting in a great improvement in the security of LLM agents, while not burdening them with significant computing costs. It further highlights the importance of security layers before deploying LLM agents to the real world as the input they receive can be adversarial and continuously change, requiring a mixture of machine learning and structured control to ensure they remain safe and reliable across different application areas. Scalable AI systems deployment safety improvements involve multi-agent security, real-time learning, and multimodal prompt injection detection in the future.

title: Multi-Agent LLM Systems: Memory Management, Coordination Failures and Semantic Conflict Resolution
abstract: As large language model (LLM) systems move from using one agent at a time to working with multiple agents together, keeping the system stable and ensuring memory stays accurate is still a major challenge. Making linear tasks work with multiple agents hurts performance by up to 70% because of extra communication and problems that spread out, but tasks that can be done at the same time can improve performance by up to 81% (Kim et al., 2025). Right now, the memory management tools we use like flat conversation logs, RAG retrieval and single-agent versioning systems (Wu et al., 2025; Su et al., 2026) do not work well when there are conflicts in open-domain semantic merges. They either need strict locks or special compilers for specific domains to handle these issues. To tackle these bottlenecks, this review paper brings together real-world failure categories, system-level checks and memory designs. It introduces a Git-managed multi-agent framework that includes dynamic task assignment, secure branch execution in isolated environments and external oversight using an LLM as a judge, along with council-based meaning-based decision making. In the end, we identify and outline the main research questions that still need to be addressed in areas like sharing experiences between different agents, figuring out the causes of faults and resolving conflicts in meaning.

title: Resource-sensitive certification of tool-augmented agent swarms: Coalgebraic semantics and LangGraph validation
abstract: Tool-augmented agent frameworks expose routing, tool calls, shared state, and execution logs, but a recorded run does not by itself establish that permissions, budgets, provenance, and audit obligations were respected. We present a certification architecture for agent swarms in which coalgebra models observable state-based execution and a Subexponential Linear Logic-labelled ledger classifies reusable and consumable evidence. The contribution is the connection between these layers: certification filters raw executions into those satisfying graph, permission, budget, append-only memory, provenance, audit-freshness, and answer-support conditions. For the implemented six-rule fragment, certified finite paths form a prefix-closed sublanguage of raw behaviour; local rule soundness yields finite-run resource preservation. We implement an indexed, transactional trace checker for that certificate language, along with an adapter that captures native version-2 streams from three deterministic LangGraph 1.2.11 StateGraph workflows without a language model or commercial API. The checker matched all expectations in a 19-trace conformance suite, accepting five positive traces and rejecting fourteen negative controls. It accepted all three unmodified framework executions and rejected all 42 controlled mutations, with one expected violation code at the mutated step in each case. A scaling sanity check covered traces from 10 to 10,000 events with seven measured repetitions per size. These results establish executable trace certification and framework-integration feasibility for the studied deterministic setting; they do not establish factual correctness, adversarial security, or production-scale generality.

title: BrandEval: A Two-Track Multi-Agent Benchmark for Risk-Sensitive LLM Crisis Communication
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP (Findings of EMNLP)
abstract: Evaluating LLMs for crisis communication requires more than judging isolated responses, because public feedback and competitor actions can reshape trust over time. Existing benchmarks remain largely static and single-turn, offering limited evidence about long-horizon risk-sensitive communication. We introduce \textbf{BrandEval}, a two-track benchmark for product-crisis communication, focusing on public brand responses to product-related safety, quality, service, and trust incidents. BrandEval-Static evaluates stakeholder-aware strategic analysis, while BrandEval-Dynamic stress-tests response policies in \textbf{BrandPolis}, a controlled multi-agent sandbox with consumer feedback, competitor responses, and trust-risk trajectories. We also construct \textbf{BrandSRD}, a Chinese crisis-response dataset, and instantiate a reference Strategic Agent using \textbf{Strategic Rationale (SR)}. Across proprietary and open-source models, we find that static strategic quality is informative but incomplete: it aligns with some end-state outcomes but does not reliably predict volatility and delayed recovery; dynamic stress tests further expose tail-risk failures under manipulative or weakly grounded policies. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/htgan-ai/BrandEval.

title: A Multi-Agent LLM Architecture with Dynamic Cascading for On-Premises, LGPD-Compliant Organizational Assistants
venue: Anais do Workshop-Escola de Sistemas de Agentes, seus Ambientes e Aplicações (WESAAC)
abstract: A integração de modelos de linguagem de grande porte (LLMs) em ambientes organizacionais que tratam dados sensíveis enfrenta duas barreiras: restrições regulatórias (no Brasil, a LGPD) e a heterogeneidade das cargas de trabalho. Este trabalho apresenta uma arquitetura multi-agente de LLMs que combina execução totalmente local com um roteador dinâmico em cascata: um roteador heurístico, quatro agentes LLM especializados (Tier 1 a Tier 3), um agente de RAG isolado por workspace, um de auditoria e um de desempenho. O roteador despacha cada consulta ao agente mais barato capaz de respondêla, com fallback transparente em caso de falha, e o sistema foi publicado como código aberto.

title: "AgentFault-500: A Labeled Dataset of Clean and Fault-Injected Multi-Agent LLM Trajectories for Failure Diagnosis"
abstract: "AgentFault-500 is a labeled dataset of execution trajectories from multi-agent LLM systems, built to evaluate failure detection, root-cause localization and diagnosis of agent faults. It contains 660 trajectories (5,661 steps): 160 clean baseline trajectories and 500 fault-injected trajectories. Each trajectory records the ordered steps of a four-agent LangGraph workflow (retrieval, researcher, reviewer, answer), including LLM calls, retrieval, tool calls and results, and agent handoffs. Faults were injected with 19 operators covering 19 of 20 types in a six-category taxonomy: Planning, Tool, Knowledge, Multi-Agent, Control and Security. Every injected record carries a ground-truth fault type, the origin step, and a root-cause flag on the faulty step. A companion replay file pairs each injected trajectory with its baseline and gives per-check scores, success deltas and a step-level fault propagation graph. Trajectories were generated deterministically (seed 42) with a mock LLM and mocked tools at temperature 0.0, so the dataset is fully reproducible. AgentFault-500 supports fault detection, taxonomy classification, root-cause localization, counterfactual analysis and early failure prediction."

title: Replication Package for Metamorphic Testing of LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: AgentMorph-MT is a metamorphic testing framework designed to evaluate the reliability and correctness of large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems. The research introduces 38 metamorphic relations to identify interaction-level failures involving agent coordination, communication, temporal sequencing, and emergent collective behavior. The framework is evaluated across multiple LLMs, multi-agent frameworks, and application scenarios, including software code review and legal contract analysis. This replication package provides the source code, test scenarios, experimental configurations, and results to support reproducibility and further research.

title: Perspective Chapter: Governing the Autonomous Fortress – Multi-Agent AI Systems for Secure and Resilient Cloud Cybersecurity
abstract: Cybersecurity is changing from reactive, human-centered systems to highly autonomous cyber-capable agents (HACCAs) that can operate at machine speed and scale. This chapter introduces the Autonomous Fortress, an architectural framework that changes artificial intelligence from a tool that only supports analysis into a system that can make decisions, plan multiple steps, use different tools, and improve its actions through continuous reasoning. The core of the Autonomous Fortress is a large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent system (MAS). In this system, specialized agents for perception, correlation, analysis, and response work together as digital teammates to protect the environment. The framework combines different coordination methods, including a hierarchical supervisor model and swarm-based dynamic handoff, to support adaptive and context-aware decision-making. This approach goes beyond traditional machine learning systems that mainly depend on fixed rules and pattern matching. Although these secure-by-design mechanisms improve the defender’s ability to respond to cyber threats, high levels of autonomy also introduce new risks, such as prompt injection, memory poisoning, and cascading system failures. Based on national cybersecurity strategies and enterprise deployments from 2025 to 2026, this chapter presents both a technical and governance roadmap for building secure and resilient autonomous cyber defense systems in modern digital and cloud-native environments.

title: Safety-constrained and runtime-assured LLM multi-agent decision making for intelligent vehicle systems
abstract: Large language models offer flexible semantic reasoning for intelligent-vehicle interfaces, but probabilistic outputs, multi-agent disagreement, and provider failures complicate safety-sensitive use. We developed SCI-Proposed-v1.0, a lightweight multi-agent semantic decision architecture that combines transparent risk-informed routing with an independent Safety Validator and deterministic local Runtime Fallback. The system produces canonical semantic actions rather than trajectories or direct vehicle-control commands. In a frozen confirmatory benchmark of 150 unseen Base Scenarios, each represented by three reviewed language variants, SCI-Proposed completed 360/450 inputs (80.0%), compared with 169/450 (37.6%) for EI-MAS and 155/450 (34.4%) for a Single LLM. Language variants were treated as repeated observations within each Base Scenario, and all methods used the same frozen model configuration. Base-scenario paired differences were 0.4244 (95% confidence interval, 0.3489-0.5000; p < 0.001) and 0.4556 (95% confidence interval, 0.3800-0.5311; p < 0.001), respectively. Complete Safety Requirement Satisfaction was 316/360 (87.8%) versus 101/360 (28.1%) for EI-MAS. In frozen ablation, removing the Safety Validator reduced its prespecified endpoint by 0.2767 (p < 0.001), and removing Runtime Fallback reduced represented-failure recovery by 0.3667 (p = 0.00195). Exact three-of-three canonical action-set stability was 27/30 (90.0%). In prespecified isolated-sandbox hardware-in-the-loop validation, Scientific Task Success was 25/30, Safety Enforcement Success was 7/7 applicable cases, and Runtime Recovery was 4/6 applicable cases. Across these complementary, prespecified stages, separating generative reasoning from independent safety validation and class-bounded local runtime recovery materially improved semantic-decision dependability under the tested qwen-plus/DashScope configuration, frozen semantic policy, and represented fault classes. These findings do not establish broader vehicle-system safety, physical-control reliability, arbitrary-fault recovery, or deployment readiness.

title: Recursive Adversarial Engine: A Stability-Oriented Architecture for Reliable Large Language Model Multi-Agent Systems
venue: International Journal of Advanced AI Applications
abstract: Large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems are rapidly migrating from laboratory prototypes to production deployments in finance, scientific research, industrial digital twins, and urban scheduling. As deployment scales, however, a family of systemic pathologies persists: decision oscillation driven by zero-sum agent interactions, cascade propagation of hallucinated content, long-horizon behavioral drift, value misalignment, and unresolved inter-agent conflict. Existing orchestration paradigms, which rely on instruction dispatch, greedy optimization, or static rules, address only shallow coordination and provide no principled mechanism for convergence. This paper proposes the Recursive Adversarial Engine (RAE), a runtime architecture for multi-agent systems organized around three propositions: bounded adversarial interaction supplies the error-detection signal, recursive correction supplies the error-elimination mechanism, and dynamic checks and balances supply the stability guarantee. We specify a four-layer reference architecture comprising adversarial verification, recursive correction, checks-and-balances scheduling, and steady-state output, and we characterize its convergence behavior through a Lyapunov-style stability argument. A qualitative comparison with self-play, multi-agent debate, alignment, and consensus frameworks delineates the paradigm difference. Engineering implications for high-stakes domains, long-horizon robustness, auditability, and middleware integration are analyzed, and open challenges are identified.

title: SGAgent : Suggestion-Guided LLM-Based Multi-Agent Framework for Repository-Level Software Repair
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has led to the emergence of intelligent agents capable of autonomously interacting with environments and invoking external tools. Recently, agent-based software repair approaches have received widespread attention, as repair agents can automatically analyze and localize bugs, generate patches, and achieve state-of-the-art performance on repository-level benchmarks (e.g., SWE-Bench). However, existing software repair approaches usually adopt a localize-then-fix paradigm , jumping directly from “where the bug is” to “how to fix it,” leaving a fundamental reasoning gap. To this end, we propose SGAgent , a S uggestion- G uided multi- Agent framework for repository-level software repair, which follows a localize-suggest-fix paradigm. Specifically, SGAgent introduces a suggestion to strengthen the transition from localization to repair. The suggester starts from the buggy locations and incrementally retrieves relevant context until it fully understands the bug, and then provides actionable repair suggestions. Moreover, we construct a Knowledge Graph (KG) from the target repository and develop a KG-based toolkit to enhance SGAgent ’s ability to enhance global contextual awareness and repository-level reasoning. Based on these components, three specialized sub-agents in SGAgent (i.e., localizer, suggester, and fixer) collaborate to achieve automated end-to-end software repair. We evaluated SGAgent on the SWE-Bench-Lite benchmark. Experimental results show that SGAgent with Claude-3.5 achieves 51.3% repair accuracy, 81.2% file-level, and 52.4% function-level localization accuracy with an average cost of $1.48 per instance, outperforming all baselines using the same base model. Moreover, SGAgent generalizes well across different base LLMs, further reaching a 60.7% resolution rate with Claude-4. When extended to vulnerability repair, SGAgent achieves a 48.0% resolution rate on VUL4J and VJBench, demonstrating strong generalization across tasks and programming languages.

title: GuardrailAgent: An Agentic Framework for Jailbreak Defense
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP (Findings of EMNLP)
abstract: Despite undergoing safety training to align with human values, large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that circumvent built-in safeguards and elicit malicious behaviors given by the adversary. Existing defenses are mostly static and fail to adapt to new or unknown attack strategies, providing limited resilience. To address these, we propose a multi-agent defense framework, GuardrailAgent, that offers adaptive, end-to-end protection. The system autonomously gathers and summarizes attack characteristics into a continuously updated knowledge base that supports both input- and output-side detection. A feedback module integrates misclassified cases for iterative improvement at minimal cost. Tested on over ten representative jailbreaks, the framework achieved a 93.1% input-side detection rate, 93.9% overall detection, and a 95.8% F1 score, while rapidly adapting to unseen attacks. These results demonstrate GuardrailAgent's outstanding capability to maintain LLM safety in the face of evolving jailbreak tactics.

title: MULTI-AGENT AI SYSTEMS FOR AUTONOMOUS SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT
venue: International Journal of Progressive Research in Engineering Management and Science
abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents, Large Language Models (LLM), and the use of multi-agents are quickly changing the landscape of software engineering by making more software development methods more automated.With the increasing complexity of software systems, there is an increasing demand of intelligent systems that can automatically aid requirements analysis, software design, code generation, testing, debugging, documentation, deployment and maintenance.A promising trend has been to delegate these tasks to Multi-Agent AI Systems which allocate these duties to autonomous agents which communicate, plan tasks, examine the output of other autonomous agents and enhance their software artifacts through iterative improvement.This paper explores the role and capabilities of Multi-agent AI in autonomous software engineering, along with the benefits and challenges in the form of a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) and comparative analysis of recent studies on the autonomous software development using a LLM and multi-agent systems.The results suggest that multi-agent systems can allocate software engineering tasks among specialized agents, which eliminates the reliance on a single AI system and can serve the purpose of requirements analysis, planning, code generation, testing, debugging, code review and documentation (Rasheed et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024).Examples of such frameworks as ChatDev, AutoGen Studio, AutoDev, CodePori, and Magentic-One show various methods of coordinating agents and performing independent tasks (Tufano et al., 2024;Dibia et al., 2024).Task separation, software quality assurance, and workflow automation can be enhanced with the help of collaborative agent architectures, but their efficiency will largely rely on communication standards, coordination, context management, and evaluation objectives (Talebirad and Nadiri, 2023; Manish, 2024).The common obstacles consist of hallucinated/untrusted code, unreliable inter-agent communication, physical security threats, computational expenses, little human control, and the inability to confidently assess autonomous-development procedures (Suri et al., 2023).In general, Multi-Agent AI has a great potential to transform AI-assisted software engineering to more autonomous development cycles, yet careful validation, proper governance, and meaningful human oversight is a necessary requirement to ensure effective and safe adoption.

title: M3MAD-Bench: Multi-Dimensional Evaluation of Multi-Agent Debate Across Domains and Modalities
venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)
abstract: As an agent-level reasoning and coordination paradigm, Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) orchestrates multiple agents through structured debate to improve answer quality and support complex reasoning. However, existing research on MAD suffers from two fundamental limitations: evaluations are conducted under fragmented and inconsistent settings, making fair comparison difficult, and are largely confined to text-only scenarios, leaving its effectiveness in multimodal settings underexplored. To address these gaps, we introduce M3MAD-Bench , a unified and extensible benchmark for evaluating MAD methods across M ulti-domain tasks, M ulti-modal inputs, and M ulti-dimensional metrics. M3MAD-Bench establishes standardized protocols over five core task domains, including Knowledge, Mathematics, Medicine, Natural Sciences, and Complex Reasoning, covering a total of 13 datasets, and systematically includes both pure text and vision-language data, enabling controlled cross-modality comparison. We evaluate MAD methods on 9 base models spanning different architectures, scales, and modality capabilities. Beyond accuracy, M3MAD-Bench incorporates efficiency-oriented metrics such as token consumption and inference time, providing a holistic view of performance--cost trade-offs. Through extensive experiments, we derive nine key insights, revealing that MAD is not uniformly effective: collaborative methods are generally more robust than adversarial ones, especially on reasoning-intensive and multimodal tasks, but often incur substantial efficiency costs. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting and designing MAD strategies in real-world applications. We believe M3MAD-Bench offers a reliable foundation for future research on standardized and reproducible MAD evaluation. The code is available at ~https://github.com/liaolea/M3MAD-Bench.

title: SentinelX AI: A Post-Quantum Secured Multi-Agent Defense Framework for LLM-Enabled Systems Against Adversarial Prompt and Agent Attacks
venue: Frontiers in artificial intelligence and applications
abstract: Large Language Model based support systems are increasingly used in many real world applications. These systems remain vulnerable to attacks such as prompt injection, tool hijacking, memory poisoning, RAG poisoning and multi agent infection. Also communication between agents may be exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL) attacks from future quantum adversaries. Existing solutions generally address only individual threats and do not provide a unified framework for securing both the LLM workflow and inter agent communication. Our paper presents SentinelX AI, a post quantum secured multi agent defense framework that examines each request before it reaches the LLM. Our developed framework consists of six processing stages including a Trust Score (TS) based risk assessment module, a blacklist based Memory Sanitizer, a controlled Attack Simulator and an Execution Gate for decision making. To protect communication between agents where SentinelX AI employs ML-KEM-512 (NIST FIPS 203) for key establishment and AES-256-GCM for authenticated encryption at every agent boundary.SentinelX AI reduces the Attack Success Rate from 73.0% to 4.0%, achieves an Attack Detection Rate of 96.0% with zero false positives, maintains a Task Success Rate of 91.3% and yields a Defense Effectiveness Score (DES) of 0.876, while introducing an average post quantum communication overhead of only 3.71 ms per agent hop (0.40% of the LLM inference time). SentinelX AI enhances the security of multi agent LLM systems with minimal additional computational cost.

title: Multi-Agent Orchestration & Conflict Resolution: Solving Coordination Challenges in Parallel Agentic Systems
venue: International Journal of Engineering Science and Information Technology
abstract: As autonomous artificial intelligence agents become more sophisticated and prevalent in enterprise systems, organizations increasingly deploy multiple specialized agents that operate in parallel on shared workflows. This practice creates a new architectural challenge: coordinating concurrent agents while preventing conflicts and preserving system integrity. Agents may generate competing recommendations, pursue misaligned optimization goals, or take actions that violate enterprise governance policies. This paper examines multi-agent orchestration and conflict resolution as a distinct architectural discipline. The study presents a four-layer orchestration model comprising agent decision-making, conflict evaluation, deterministic resolution, and committed execution. It then compares how three contemporary frameworks, LangGraph, LangChain, and CrewAI, implement this model through different abstractions. Four conflict-resolution mechanisms are also examined: priority-based, policy-aligned, consensus-based, and utility-maximizing. Their underlying logic is formalized through three analytical constructs. The first is a policy-compliant utility maximization model. The second is a consensus quorum threshold grounded in established Byzantine fault tolerance theory. The third is a layered orchestration latency model that explains why hierarchical decomposition improves scalability. These formalizations are presented as structural models rather than measured benchmark results. The analysis shows that each framework favors a different coordination style, that each resolution mechanism offers distinct trade-offs between speed, fairness, and governance assurance, and that hierarchical decomposition reduces coordination overhead as the number of agents grows. The paper concludes that coordination challenges introduced by parallel agents are not obstacles but opportunities for architectural sophistication. Organizations must therefore select orchestration architectures aligned with their governance requirements, scale targets, and operational complexity, rather than adopting a single framework by default

title: Interaction Persistence and Adversarial Propagation in Multi-Agent Educational LLM Systems
venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on AI Research.
abstract: Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in educational applications such as tutoring, explanation generation, and automated assessment, yet safety research has largely examined single-turn interactions, leaving open how adversarial influence propagates through the persistent memory and feedback mechanisms of educational multi-agent systems. We investigate three research questions: how interaction persistence affects adversarial propagation, which shared mechanisms enable it, and how educational task characteristics and lightweight defences moderate it. We evaluate a unified three-phase interaction framework across pedagogical explanation generation (BloomXplain), automated essay assessment (ASAP), and dialogic tutoring (ConvoLearn), using Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-32B with representative prompt injection attacks and verifier-based defences. Results show that interaction persistence does not uniformly amplify adversarial influence: propagation emerges primarily through repeated reuse of evaluator-generated optimization objectives, while tasks with stronger semantic boundaries resist cross-instance propagation. Verifier-based defences interrupt recursive propagation but can suppress legitimate feedback, revealing a security-utility trade-off. These findings suggest educational AI safety evaluation should jointly consider interaction persistence, propagation mechanism, and utility preservation rather than relying solely on prompt-level robustness evaluation. Research artifact: code and data are available at https://github.com/wentinghu2025/edu-mas-attack-propagation; an interactive results explorer is available at https://wentinghu2025.github.io/edu-mas-attack-propagation/

title: Hallucination to Consensus: Multi-Agent LLMs for End-to-End JUnit Test Generation
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
abstract: Unit testing plays a critical role in ensuring software correctness. However, writing unit tests manually is labor-intensive, especially for strongly typed languages like Java, motivating the need for automated approaches. Traditional methods primarily rely on search-based or randomized algorithms to generate tests that achieve high code coverage and produce regression oracles, which are assertions derived from the program’s current behavior rather than its intended functionality. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled oracle generation from natural language descriptions, aligning better with user requirements. However, existing LLM-based methods often require LLM fine-tuning or rely on external tools such as EvoSuite for test prefix generation, making them costly or cumbersome to apply in practice. In this work, we propose CANDOR, a novel end-to-end, prompt engineering-based LLM framework for automated unit test generation in Java. CANDOR orchestrates multiple specialized LLM agents to collaboratively generate complete JUnit tests, including both high-quality test prefixes and accurate oracles. To mitigate the notorious hallucinations in LLMs and improve oracle correctness, we introduce a novel strategy that engages multiple reasoning LLMs in a panel discussion and generates accurate oracles based on consensus. Additionally, to reduce the verbosity of reasoning LLMs’ outputs, we propose a novel dual-LLM pipeline to produce concise and structured oracle evaluations. Our experiments on the HumanEvalJava and more complex LeetCodeJava datasets show that CANDOR is comparable with EvoSuite in generating tests with high code coverage and clearly superior in terms of mutation score. Moreover, our prompt engineering-based approach CANDOR significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art, fine-tuning-based oracle generator TOGLL by at least 21.1 percentage points in oracle correctness on both correct and faulty source code. Further ablation studies confirm the critical contributions of key agents in improving test prefix quality and oracle accuracy.

title: AI-Driven Personal and Collaborative Task Management: A Survey of Intelligent Scheduling, LLM Agents, and Multi-Agent Systems
venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming traditional productivity and task management systems by enabling intelligent assistance for task planning, prioritization, scheduling, collaboration, and decision-making. This paper presents a survey of AI-driven personal and collaborative productivity systems, focusing on intelligent task management, scheduling, meeting management, large language models (LLMs), AI agents, multi-agent systems, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Existing research is reviewed and classified according to the AI techniques employed, application areas, system capabilities, and limitations. The survey examines how these technologies support individual productivity as well as collaborative workflows involving tasks, calendars, meetings, communication, and shared knowledge. A comparative analysis is presented to identify the strengths and limitations of existing approaches. The study further highlights key research gaps, including fragmented productivity tools, limited contextual awareness and personalization, challenges in autonomous task execution and multi-agent coordination, and concerns related to privacy, security, reliability, and human oversight. Finally, emerging trends and future research directions are discussed toward developing more integrated, adaptive, trustworthy, and context-aware AI-driven productivity systems. This survey provides a structured understanding of the current research landscape and identifies opportunities for advancing intelligent productivity and task management systems. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Productivity Management, Task Management, Intelligent Scheduling, Large Language Models, AI Agents, Multi-Agent Systems, Human-AI Collaboration, Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

title: Beyond Final Answers: Auditing Trajectory-Level Hallucinations in Multi-Agent Industrial Workflows
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that reason, use tools, and act over multiple steps. Yet most hallucination benchmarks still evaluate only the final output, missing failures that originate in intermediate Thought-Action-Observation steps. We present Trajel, a dataset and evaluation framework for auditing trajectory-level hallucinations in multi-agent industrial workflows. Trajel introduces a five-type hallucination taxonomy (factual, referential, logical, procedural, and scope-based) over expert-annotated agent traces from AssetOpsBench. We benchmark supervised detection models at the subtask, trajectory, and long-context levels. Our results show that the most common failure modes are missed by existing benchmarks, that nearly half of hallucinated trajectories involve multiple types at once, and that automated detectors with high binary accuracy still misclassify the subtlest types. Trajectory-aware detection significantly outperforms standard post-hoc verification, making taxonomy-grounded evaluation necessary for safer agentic deployment.

title: Understanding Conversational Patterns in Multi-agent Programming: A Case Study on Fibonacci Game Development
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to software engineering (SE), yet their potential for autonomous, role-oriented collaboration remains largely underexplored. Understanding how multiple LLM-based agents coordinate, maintain role alignment, and converge on solutions is critical for SE, as naively allowing agents to interact does not reliably lead to correct or stable outcomes. Recent empirical studies show that unstructured or poorly understood interaction dynamics can result in error propagation, premature consensus on incorrect solutions, or prolonged disagreement that prevents convergence, even when correct partial solutions are present early in the interaction. As an initial step towards addressing this underexplored area, we undertake a systematic analysis of conversations between two agents, a Designer and a Programmer across 12 model combinations from 7 open-source LLMs (Gemma 2, Gemma 3, LLaMA 3.2, LLaMA 3.3, DeepSeek-R1, MiniCPM, and Qwen3). Our systematic approach reveals three key dimensions of multi-agent interaction: efficiency (the speed and stability of convergence), consistency (the degree of role alignment visualized by BLEU and ROUGE), and effectiveness (the extent of compilation success and error resolution). Results show that the DeepSeek-R1:DeepSeek-R1 pair was unique in converging to the correct solution from the very first iteration and sustaining it consistently to the final iteration, while LLaMA 3.2:LLaMA 3.2 and Qwen3:Qwen3 demonstrated strong Designer:Programmer role alignment despite of diverging from the correct solution. The other pairs deviated from the task, never to converge to a result. These findings advance understanding of agentic programming and highlight the need for further research on understanding and calibrating convergence and stop conditions essential for future autonomous SE.

title: Automated Detection and Classification of Delusion-related Content in Naturalistic Audio Diaries Using Multi-Agent Language Models
abstract: Speech monologues recorded in naturalistic settings provide opportunities to characterize mental illness phenomenology and detect symptom exacerbation. Large language models (LLMs) offer new possibilities for automating this process, as they require annotated data primarily for evaluation rather than training. In this paper, we present a novel automated, multi-agent LLM pipeline for the fine-grained, multi-label extraction of language suggestive of delusional beliefs, associated affective responses, and behavioral responses from transcripts of naturalistic audio diaries collected from people with moderate persecutory ideation. Evaluating an ensemble of three foundation models, we demonstrate that detailed diagnostic prompt instructions successfully reduce false positives for delusional theme classification, but also constrain the interpretation of affective or behavioral responses. Furthermore, comparing multi-agent adjudication frameworks shows that complex conversational debate between agents diminishes accuracy on clinically ambiguous text by inducing premature consensus. Instead, majority voting establishes robust performance (Micro F1 of 0.872 and 0.779 for delusion detection and classification respectively). This work provides a validated and scalable pipeline for the automated detection and characterization of content suggesting delusional beliefs in naturalistic speech.

title: DarkForest: Less Talk, Higher Accuracy for Multi-Agent LLMs
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems improve reasoning by combining outputs from multiple agents, but interaction-heavy methods can introduce error propagation and high communication overhead. When agents exchange raw responses or reasoning traces, incorrect intermediate reasoning may be adopted and amplified, leading to confident but wrong consensus; multi-round communication also increases token consumption, latency, and inference cost. In this paper, we propose a controlled-communication coordination framework named DarkForest. DarkForest first keeps agents independent, so each agent produces an answer without seeing the others' outputs. It then parses the raw responses into structured candidate records, groups semantically equivalent candidates into clusters, and estimates a calibrated belief distribution over these clusters using agent reliability, confidence, parse quality, support-pattern reliability, and independence corrections. A coordinator receives only policy-permitted evidence from this belief state with controlled communication. Experiments on six reasoning benchmarks show that DarkForest achieves leading overall quality, improves the strongest baseline by up to 30.7\% on benchmark metrics, and reduces token consumption by up to $6.5\times$ compared with communication-heavy baselines.

title: Trust but Verify: Prover-Verifier Deliberation for Selective LLM Prediction
abstract: Reliably knowing when a language model is correct is almost as important as being correct. We introduce prover-verifier deliberation (PVD), an inference-time protocol grounded in interactive proof theory, as a mechanism for selective prediction: the protocol produces both an answer and a structured confidence verdict, allowing a system to report high-confidence answers while abstaining on uncertain cases. In each dialogue, a prover defends a candidate answer through checkable sub-claims while a verifier issues targeted challenges and returns \textsc{Accept}, \textsc{Challenge}, or \textsc{Reject}. Because frozen language models are imperfect provers and verifiers operating over a noisy channel, formal soundness and completeness guarantees do not transfer; instead, we characterize the protocol empirically through its coverage-precision behavior. Our main experiment uses Claude Sonnet 4.6 as prover and Claude Haiku 4.5 as verifier on GPQA Diamond. Questions accepted with no answer revision, which we call Accept + No Change (ANC), are reported as the high-confidence subset; we evaluate this subset by its precision and coverage. ANC separates reliable from unreliable answers, yielding a $\sim$30pp HC-Prec gap over the non-ANC complement. Robustness experiments with GPT and Gemini pairings show that high HC-Prec can transfer across model families, while verifier strictness and domain competence largely determine the size of the selection gap. On Humanity's Last Exam, weaker prover-verifier pairings can collapse or invert the ANC signal, illustrating a practical failure mode when the verifier operates outside its effective region. Comparisons with self-consistency, universal self-consistency, multi-agent debate, and Reflexion suggest that prover-verifier deliberation supplies a distinct argument-defensibility signal for selective prediction.

title: Security of OpenClaw Agents: Fundamentals, Attacks, and Countermeasures
abstract: The rapid evolution of large language model (LLM)-driven autonomous agents has given rise to OpenClaw, a new class of open-source agent frameworks that operate as continuously running, skill-augmented systems with persistent memory, multi-channel interaction, and high degrees of autonomy. Such capabilities enable OpenClaw agents to autonomously execute complex, multi-step tasks and interact seamlessly with external applications, but simultaneously introduce a substantially enlarged attack surface. In particular, the combination of high-privilege operations and persistent memory exposes OpenClaw agents to various emerging threats, including skill poisoning, cognitive manipulation, multi-agent cascading failures, and supply-chain vulnerabilities. In this survey, we present a comprehensive study of the security landscape of OpenClaw agents. We first examine the general architecture and key characteristics that distinguish OpenClaw agents from traditional AI agent systems. We categorize existing security and privacy threats into a layered framework and analyze how vulnerabilities arise during agent reasoning, action execution, and external interaction. Representative defense mechanisms are also reviewed to draw the current defense landscape. Finally, several unresolved issues related to the reliability and trustworthiness of OpenClaw ecosystems are discussed.
